presentingComplaint: Progressive facial puffiness and bilateral leg swelling with frothy urine over 3 weeks
history: Previously well 34-year-old man with 3 weeks of insidious periorbital puffiness (worst on waking) progressing to pitting pedal and pretibial edema, abdominal fullness, and persistently frothy urine. Reports weight gain of ~5 kg and reduced exertional tolerance. No gross hematuria, dysuria, or flank pain. No recent sore throat, rash, joint pains, or diarrheal illness. No NSAID abuse, no known diabetes or hypertension, no recent travel. Family history unremarkable.
examination: Alert, comfortable at rest, not toxic. Marked periorbital edema and bilateral pitting edema to the knees; mild shifting dullness suggesting early ascites. Pertinent negatives: no rash, no purpura, no synovitis, no lymphadenopathy, no raised JVP, chest clear with no basal crackles of cardiac failure, no hepatosplenomegaly, no CVA tenderness. No focal neurological deficit.

labs.urine microscopy: oval fat bodies / fatty casts, no dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys with preserved corticomedullary differentiation and no obstruction; small-volume ascites noted
differentialDiagnoses: Nephrotic syndrome (primary glomerular, e.g. minimal change / membranous / FSGS)
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs given proteinuria/glomerular disease
Use loop diuretics cautiously to avoid intravascular volume depletion and AKI
ACE-inhibitor/ARB for antiproteinuric effect - monitor creatinine and potassium
Statin caution if concurrent hepatic disease
edgeCases: Nephrotic-range proteinuria markedly raises venous and arterial thromboembolic risk (renal vein thrombosis, PE) - sudden flank pain or dyspnea should prompt imaging
In adults membranous nephropathy and FSGS are common; minimal change dominates in children - biopsy usually needed in adults
Secondary causes (diabetes, SLE, amyloid, hepatitis B/C, malignancy) must be excluded before labelling primary
expectedMaiK: This is a classic nephrotic syndrome: heavy (nephrotic-range) proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia with a bland urinary sediment and preserved renal function. Prioritise secondary-cause screening and renal biopsy, start antiproteinuric RAAS blockade plus a statin, and counsel on the elevated thromboembolic risk.
expectedNextQuestions: Any frothy urine, and how heavy is the proteinuria (quantify with uPCR / 24h urine)?
Features of a secondary cause - diabetes, recent infection, rash/arthralgia, hepatitis risk factors, new medications, or symptoms of malignancy?
Any calf pain, unilateral leg swelling, or breathlessness suggesting venous thromboembolism?
expectedInvestigations: Quantify proteinuria (uPCR or 24h urine) with serum albumin and lipids
Secondary-cause serology: fasting glucose/HbA1c, ANA, complement (C3/C4), HBsAg/anti-HCV, serum/urine electrophoresis
Renal biopsy for histological diagnosis in an adult
regressionAssertions: bland sediment with nephrotic-range proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia should rank nephrotic above glomerulonephritis
